P-001P-001 Iconic powersA power is iconic when one image tells you whose it is, so it is built from a familiar idea made strange or from one repeatable signature.2026-09-04
P-002P-002 Simple powersOne mechanism used cleverly beats a toolbox chosen from, because an audience can only feel tension when it already knows what the power can do.2026-09-05
P-003P-003 Earned progressionA power-up is only satisfying when the audience has watched the bill being paid, in time, training, sacrifice or death.2026-09-04

P-005P-005 A group of individualsA villain group is one force made of people you could each pick out of a line-up, and a member you have no screen time to make a person weakens the group; a faceless collective is a deliberate choice, never a default.2026-09-05
P-006P-006 Every villain leaves a markEvery member of a villain group changes the heroes' story in a way no other member does; if two members leave the same mark, one of them is a wall, not a villain.2026-09-05
P-007P-007 A group you can seeThe eye reads a group as a unit before the plot does, through a shared uniform, symbol or palette that each member's own silhouette still stands out inside; drop the shared mark and the group stops existing on screen.2026-09-05
P-008P-008 Rules before rescueA power may solve a conflict only to the degree the audience already understands it; a power the audience does not understand may create problems and never solve them.2026-09-05

S-001, S-002, S-003 (Pavelover, one family) and S-004 (Brandon Sanderson, a produced author, the second family), so the agreements marked cross-family below are the first in the library that are not one channel agreeing with itself

Contents
  1. What the sources agree on
  2. How the principles interlock
  3. What Hood Ninjaz has and lacks
  4. Directions Vision can see
  5. Questions the next intakes could answer
  6. Ingested so far

What the sources agree on

Four sources, two families, three subjects: how a protagonist's power is built, how a villain group is built, and how a whole system of powers earns its place in a story. Read together they argue one thing from three sides. The audience must be able to read it without being told, and a power may only be spent on the plot once it has been read. A power is read by one image (P-001) and one mechanism (P-002). A cost is read by watching it paid (P-003) and by never seeing it vanish (P-004). A group is read by one shared mark (P-007), a member by a silhouette the mark cannot swallow (P-007) and by the one change they make to a hero (P-006), and a roster by whether the story had time to make each member a person (P-005). A system is read before it resolves anything (P-008), and a world is read through what its few systems do to ordinary life rather than through how many systems it has (P-009).

The cross-family agreement (new with S-004). The critic and the practitioner meet on three principles. Sanderson's Second Law ("Limitations > Powers", a limitation, a weakness and a cost being three different things) is Pavelover's flaws-that-stay argument from the author's chair: P-004 is now CORROBORATED. His Mistborn push-or-pull example and "without limitations there is no innovation" are P-002's one-mechanism rule: CORROBORATED. His Third Law warning against more-is-more (one danger done well against a film whose most common criticism was that it carried too many villains) is P-005's roster-priced-by-time: CORROBORATED. The critic argues from the audience's memory; the practitioner argues from the desk; they land on the same rules, which is what corroboration is for.

The one exception the sources allow is deliberate illegibility: the faceless collective (P-005) and the soft-magic mystery (P-008), where sameness or mystery is the point. Both are legibility rules in reverse: the reader must be able to read "this is a tide, not a cast" or "this is a mystery, it will not rescue anyone" from the first appearance.

How the principles interlock

  • P-001 and P-007 are the same rule at two scales. P-001 is the image of one power tied to one character; P-007 is the image of one group. A character can pass P-001 while the group fails P-007, which is the exact shape of Face's crew in A-003.
  • P-002, P-005 and P-009 are the same budget at three scales. Attention is finite: one mechanism per power, one person per screen-time slot, one idea extrapolated per world. A toolbox power, an oversized roster and a pile of unconnected systems fail the same way: the reader stops expecting anything from the next reveal.
  • P-008 is the currency P-003 pays in. A power may resolve a conflict only to the degree the audience already understands it; the bill P-003 watches being paid is understanding spent. In Hood Ninjaz the two gaps are one: no system has been explained before it acted (A-004) and nobody has paid a visible price (A-001, A-002).
  • P-003 pays through P-006. In the model cases a villain's mark on a hero is the bill the hero pays. Villains are the mechanism by which earned progression lands, so A-003's finding that no crew member is designed to do anything to Kevin and A-001's finding that Kevin has paid no visible price are one gap seen from two pages.
  • P-004's three kinds of limit sort P-006's marks. With S-004 the cost of a power comes in three kinds (what it cannot do, what an enemy can exploit, what using it takes), and the sharpest marks a villain leaves are exploited weaknesses. Sera eating Aura is the one weakness canon has fully designed, and it belongs to an antagonist.
  • P-004 applies to an army, not only to a hero. An antagonist force whose costs vanish generation by generation is the Solo Leveling counter-example wearing a uniform. A-004 finds the TANCs have no cost of any kind, and A-003 finds they have no face and no mark, so the army fails three tests with one cause.
  • P-005's exception and P-007's exception meet on the TANCs. A faceless tide may skip individuality but not the shared mark. The TANCs have neither, so they are not yet the deliberate exception; they are the unfilled roster.
  • P-008's exception and P-004's unpayable cost meet on Kuga. A mystery may create problems and never solve them, and the only known price for stopping Kuga was paid once by ten gods and can never be paid again: canon uses the extended P-004 failure mode on purpose as the Season 3 engine, and holds Kuga to the soft-end rule until Season 2. That is the one place the library finds a deliberate tension rather than a gap.

What Hood Ninjaz has and lacks

Tokens only; the reasoning lives on the applied pages.

Has. The Power of Will as one rule with one image (Kevin, P-001 and P-002, PASSES in A-001), held to the soft-end rule by design until its reveal (P-008, PASSES in A-004), with a complete taxonomy of limits (P-004, PASSES in A-004). Five of six systems descending from one idea, Kuga and the water, with the two additions defended in terms (P-009, PASSES in A-004). Kuga's amplification with a complete taxonomy and the deliberately spent unpayable cost (P-004, PASSES in A-004). The Mandem colour trio as an owned shared mark and the burn marks as the exact P-007 shape (PASSES on shape, A-003). Bio Genetix's slogan as a corporate mark extrapolated into everyday life (P-007 PASSES in A-003, P-009 PASSES for the brand in A-004). The voodoo sensory register as a fully specified shared register (P-007, PASSES) and a designed cost (P-004, PASSES on cost). Aura's reach into society and culture, the Ninja Code and Springvale as everyday speech (P-009, PASSES on society and culture). Legible silhouettes for Face, Spike, Sleeze, Eve and Tribal (P-007, PASSES). Marks on the heroes' story from Jaden and Jon, and from Spike, Tribal, Teddy Lucas, Paul Mitchell and Dr Kane (P-006, PASSES).

Lacks. A visible price paid on screen by anyone in the ensemble, the largest AT-RISK cluster in A-002 (P-003, P-004). Any system explained to the audience before it acted on the page, and any reveal schedule at all for Aura, voodoo or the Book (P-008, AT-RISK and UNRESOLVED across A-004). Any design for the TANCs, any named unit outside Uno, and any cost a TANC pays (A-003 and A-004, UNRESOLVED and AT-RISK). A shared mark for Face's crew and any mark from the crew on Kevin (A-003, AT-RISK). Manic as a person (A-003, AT-RISK on all three tests). The three burn-mark designs while a wrist is already on the page (A-003, AT-RISK). A signature visual for Kevin (A-001) and for Uno (A-002), both AT-RISK. A flaw for Jaden, the sharpest single finding in A-002 (P-004, AT-RISK). The white thread as a mark that reaches all three of the next-gen trio (A-003, AT-RISK). Any reach of Aura into the economy or the institutions beyond one company (P-009, AT-RISK in A-004). A cost the Book charges its reader rather than the world (P-004, AT-RISK in A-004). One canon write-up for Kuga's amplification and the Power of Will instead of two (P-009, AT-RISK in A-004). A weakness an enemy could exploit in voodoo (P-004, AT-RISK in A-004).

Directions Vision can see

Vision's read, studied, not binding, never written into canon by this page. Each one names the findings it would close and the question it bears on, so Bupe can rule on the question and not on the prose.

  1. Give the TANC generations a cost ladder, the way P-004 rotates a hero's costs. Prototypes pay in orders: cut the handler and the unit stops. Adaptives pay in personality: a unit that wants something can be baited. Apexes pay in autonomy: free of Bio Genetix means free of repair, so every wound is permanent. The tide keeps its facelessness and gains a limit at every rung. Would move A-003's generation rows and A-004's TANC cost row from AT-RISK. Bears on A-003 Q7 and A-004 Q4, option (b), without deciding either.
  2. Make Face's crew the Mandem's mirror in how loyalty is marked. The Mandem carry a burn given once and never removable; the crew could carry Face's black on their kit, a mark he gives and can take back. Loyalty burned in against loyalty bought. When a member leaves, the black comes off, which is a scene. Would close A-003's shared-mark finding and give the crew a mark on the Mandem's story. Bears on A-003 Q2, option (b).
  3. Manic as the crew's own Loyalty Elixir. The one crew power that rhymes with the series' central wound is memory alteration. If Manic is the one who sees Face's cracks first and papers over them, he becomes the villain of the Season 2 memory arc and leaves a mark no other member can, and Tribal, who sees the scars the Elixir left, gets an opponent inside the same room. Would close A-003's three Manic findings. Bears on A-003 Q3, option (b).
  4. The Sonya chain as the P-006 proof. Ranked 2 is the villain who does the most and exists the least. If one Adaptive unit is named in Season 2, given a personality and allowed to climb, then arrives as ranked 2 in Season 3, the chain becomes a payoff the audience has been taught to fear. Bears on A-003 Q8, option (a), and on Q7.
  5. Kevin's first bill should be paid to a villain, after the rule is taught. A-001 says nobody has paid; S-003 says villains are how bills get paid; S-004 says the audience must hold the rule before the power resolves anything. So the order is fixed: the declaration rule reaches the audience (A-001 Q4), then the first crew member to leave a mark on Kevin costs him something the audience sees, priced by the Power of Will's own asymmetry. Spike is the natural candidate. Would open the P-003, P-006 and P-008 gaps at once.
  6. Teach Aura through Kevin in the barbershop, in a scene where the rule costs someone. The Ninja Code removes every public explainer, and P-008 forbids a rule arriving in the scene that needs it, so the one legitimate classroom is Jon teaching Kevin as the audience's proxy, and the lesson should hurt (a demonstration that costs Jon or Kevin something, not a lecture). Would move A-004's Aura row from AT-RISK. Bears on A-004 Q1, option (c).
  7. The Book's first audience contact is a problem, not a solution. The Loyalty Elixir came out of the Book and unmade the Mandem; if the audience meets the Book through what it did to three brothers before anyone reads it on screen, the system enters on P-008's soft-end terms and the Elixir's cost becomes the Book's first price. Bears on A-004 Q2 and Q6 (option (b) for the Elixir's own cost).
  8. Aura's missing economy is Face's crew's missing purpose. A-004 finds nobody sells, insures, polices or profits from Aura beyond Bio Genetix; A-003 finds the crew's marks land on nobody. One answer serves both: the crew runs the underground economy of ninja (protection, fights, the successor to Jenny), which extrapolates the system into money and gives the crew a footprint on the city Kevin lives in. Bears on A-004 Q5, option (b), and on A-003 finding 16.
  9. Eve and Sera's snake rhyme is either a defect or a seed. Two snake-coded women across two antagonist groups is a P-007 defect if accidental. It is a seed if Eve's shadow snakes are voodoo-adjacent, which the Bible's Spirit pillar does not rule out. That is a canon change and a large one, so it is A-003 Q5's option (c), not a recommendation.
  10. The library is still two thirds Naruto-side, and the show is three things. Powers, villain groups and magic systems are the Naruto half. Nothing ingested speaks to how a grounded crime season builds its bill or how satire keeps its threat. Row 8 stays aimed at a grounded-drama writing source so the library grows toward the whole show.

A power is iconic when one image tells you whose it is, so it is built from a familiar idea made strange or from one repeatable signature.

Contents
  1. Rule
  2. Why it works
  3. How to apply it
  4. The test
  5. Failure mode
  6. Evidence
  7. Disagreements
  8. In Hood Ninjaz

Rule

A power reads as iconic when a single frozen frame is enough to name the character holding it, with no face, no costume and no line of dialogue in shot. That frame gets earned one of two ways: take a power the audience already knows and give it one twist nobody else has used, or give the power one repeatable signature moment that looks the same every time and belongs to nobody else. A power that does neither is competent, never memorable, no matter how strong it is on paper.

Why it works

An audience builds identity out of pattern recognition, not out of a stat sheet. The twist route works because familiarity plus one clean deviation is easier to hold in memory than a wholly new idea explained from scratch. The signature-move route works because repetition is what makes a beat readable at a glance: once a viewer has seen it land the same way twice, the third time needs no explanation at all. Both routes are cheap to stage and expensive to imitate, which is exactly the asymmetry a long-running story needs from its most-repeated visual.

How to apply it

  1. Before naming a power, write down the one thing a reader would draw from memory to prove they had seen it before, and cut anything that does not serve that one thing.
  2. If the base idea is common (fire, strength, speed, blades), find the single specific twist that could only belong to this character, and remove every other twist competing for the same slot.
  3. Design one repeatable visual or behavioural beat that fires identically every time the power activates, and hold it unchanged from its first appearance to any later reveal built on it.
  4. Test the power against a different character doing the same job with a different toolkit; if nothing on the page needs to change, the power is interchangeable rather than iconic.

The test

  1. Could a reader identify this character from one panel of the power alone, with no name and no face shown?
  2. Is there one thing this power does or looks like that no other character in the cast is allowed to do or look like?
  3. If the power is a familiar type, does this character's specific use of it differ from every generic version of that type?
  4. Does the power have a repeatable beat, or does it look different every time it is drawn?

Failure mode

The power reads as competent rather than memorable: a reader could swap it for a same-tier power belonging to a different character and nothing about the scene would need to change. A cast built this way blurs in silhouette, because nothing about any single power is doing identification work.

Evidence

S-00101:36-02:36A wholly fresh power reads as iconic through a visually distinct look, and a power can also become iconic purely through a named, repeatable signature movesupports
S-00102:37-03:44A protagonist assembled from many other characters' ability types, with no one thing unique to him, reads as forgettable rather than iconicsupports (counter-example)
Jujutsu Kaisen Fandom-Confirms the two signature moves the source names exist as described (Kamehameha, Gojo's Unlimited Void); the craft inference is S-001's, not this source'ssupports

None yet.

One mechanism used cleverly beats a toolbox chosen from, because an audience can only feel tension when it already knows what the power can do.

Contents
  1. Rule
  2. Why it works
  3. How to apply it
  4. The test
  5. Failure mode
  6. Evidence
  7. Disagreements
  8. In Hood Ninjaz

Rule

A protagonist's power should be one mechanism the character learns to use in ever more creative ways, not a growing shelf of separate abilities picked to fit each new problem. Tension comes from the audience already knowing the mechanism's limits before the scene starts; a fight becomes a puzzle the mechanism must solve, rather than a menu the character selects from. Side characters and villains may carry a wider kit, because the audience is not asked to track their internal logic scene to scene the way it tracks the lead's.

Why it works

If a reader already understands what a power can and cannot do, every new use of it is legible as either clever or reckless, and the writer can generate surprise from application rather than from inventing a new rule on the spot. A toolbox protagonist removes that legibility: any problem can be solved by reaching for whichever tool the scene needs, so no fight can ever really threaten the character, because the audience cannot predict what is off the table. One mechanism, applied differently each time, is also cheaper to plan across a long-running story: every future problem is already answerable by the same handful of rules the audience learned on day one.

How to apply it

  1. Write the power's mechanism as a single sentence a stranger could repeat back after one scene; if the sentence needs "and" to hold every ability, the power is a kit, not a mechanism.
  2. Before writing a fight, list the specific properties the mechanism has (what it changes, what it cannot change, what it costs) and solve the scene using only that list.
  3. When a scene seems to need a new ability, first ask whether the existing mechanism can be applied in an unfamiliar way instead of adding a new one.
  4. Reserve a genuine multi-ability kit for a side character or a villain, where the audience is not expected to predict every option before it is used.

The test

  1. Can the power be described in one sentence without an "and"?
  2. When this character solves a problem, does the solution use the same underlying mechanism as every other scene, applied differently?
  3. If a new ability shows up mid-story with no earlier hint of it, is there a stated reason the mechanism now does more than it used to?
  4. Could a reader predict, before the fight starts, roughly what tools this character has available?

Failure mode

The fight loses tension because the character's option list can grow to match whatever the plot needs; a reader stops asking "how will they solve this" because the honest answer is "with whichever ability the scene requires." The mechanism stops being a character trait and becomes a plot convenience.

Evidence

SourceTimestampsWhat it arguedVerdict
S-00103:46-06:44One elastic mechanism, reapplied against very different opponents, beats a shelf of separately named abilities used one at a timesupports
S-00103:46-06:44A single transformation rule, reinterpreted per object, is simple even though its outputs vary widelysupports
S-00103:46-06:44A protagonist choosing from many separately learned abilities, rather than reapplying one, reads as less inventive even in the same fight structuresupports (counter-example)
S-004Second Law, segments 10 to 11Brandon Sanderson, writing as a produced author about his own design, argues that innovation comes from limitation rather than from the size of the power list, holding that without limitations there is no innovation. His worked case is Mistborn, where a practitioner can move only metal objects and only by pushing them directly away or pulling them directly toward the self, so every new use has to be a cleverer application of the one mechanism. He reads The Wheel of Time the same way, calling its elemental palette generic and locating the interest in the skill it takes to weave the flows into patterns.supports

Disagreements

None yet.

A power-up is only satisfying when the audience has watched the bill being paid, in time, training, sacrifice or death.

Contents
  1. Rule
  2. Why it works
  3. How to apply it
  4. The test
  5. Failure mode
  6. Evidence
  7. Disagreements
  8. In Hood Ninjaz

Rule

A power-up should land on the audience as a receipt for something already shown being spent: time passing, training endured, a sacrifice made, or a near-death survived. The size of the jump matters less than whether the audience watched the cost accrue first. A power-up with no visible cost reads as an unlock rather than a moment, because nothing on screen earned it.

Why it works

Satisfaction from a power-up is really relief that a debt has been paid, so the writer's job is to make the debt visible well before the payment. A jump that arrives with no shown cost reads as arbitrary, because the audience has nothing to measure the new strength against; the character was simply handed more. A jump that arrives after visible cost reframes the whole preceding stretch as investment rather than filler, which is why the strongest version of this beat lands hundreds of chapters, not scenes, after the story started asking for it.

How to apply it

  1. Before writing a power-up, decide what the character gives up to get it (time, a training relationship, a physical toll, a piece of themselves) and put that cost on the page before the payoff.
  2. Space power-ups apart deliberately; a jump that follows the last one too closely reads as an unlock rather than a threshold crossed.
  3. Land the power-up on an emotional peak the story has already been building toward, never on a schedule or a level marker.
  4. If a character's growth has no visible unit (an internal capacity rather than a number), design one external, visual readout for it before the audience is asked to track it.

The test

  1. Has the audience seen the character pay something specific before this power-up lands?
  2. Would a reader, looking back, be able to name the moment training or sacrifice began?
  3. Does the power-up land on an emotional beat the story has been building toward, rather than on a convenient scene?
  4. If the growth being tracked is internal, does the audience have any visible way to read it before the power-up arrives?
  5. Set beside a rival power-up on a much shorter clock, does this one still read as the slower, harder-won climb, or would a viewer struggle to tell the two apart on pacing alone?

Failure mode

The character's growth reads as a skip rather than a climb: an audience that has not watched the cost accrue receives the new power as an announcement rather than an earned moment, and the story's remaining threats feel arbitrary because there was no visible floor the character rose from.

Evidence

S-00106:45-10:15A power-up landing on one of a story's most emotional moments, hundreds of chapters after the story began asking for it, reads as satisfying because the audience watched the cost accrue in fullsupports
S-00106:45-10:15Starting a character far below every other cast member and then compressing an enormous power climb into very few episodes reads as unsatisfying, because the audience is told the journey happened rather than shown itsupports (counter-example)
S-00208:34-10:56Deku's power-up cost accrues on screen across his fight against Todoroki, where he repeatedly breaks his own finger to force a shockwave, worsening the damage to his arm each time, before he slowly learns to control the power without destroying his bodysupports

S-00205:32-08:34Sung Jin-Woo wins one major fight after another without visibly paying anything, so no single power-up in the sequence reads as a bill being settled, only as another free upgradesupports (counter-example)

Disagreements

None yet.

A drawback that can be solved was a delay, not a flaw: the cost may change as the character grows, but the power is never without one, and the limits that stay are what make a win mean anything.

Contents
  1. Rule
  2. Why it works
  3. How to apply it
  4. The test
  5. Failure mode
  6. Evidence
  7. Disagreements
  8. In Hood Ninjaz

Rule

Every power needs an active cost, though the cost does not have to be the same one forever: as a character grows, the specific limit they started with can be resolved and retired, so long as a new limit takes its place at the new tier of power. A limit that is resolved and never replaced was only ever a delay dressed as a flaw, not a real one. Whatever limit is currently in force is what makes a victory cost something and a loss survivable rather than certain; without one in force, every fight's outcome is decided by how much the plot needs the character to win.

Why it works

A cost the audience watches being paid holds tension for as long as it stays in force: every fight staged while it is live carries real stakes, because the character has not simply been handed a way around it. What drains that tension is a cost retired with nothing replacing it, since a limit gone for good teaches the audience to wait out every future limit rather than respect it. The best versions of this rule keep a cost in force at every tier, so the audience can never fully relax into assuming the character wins, no matter how strong that character becomes elsewhere, and the cheap, unlimited option is always sitting right there and always the wrong one to take.

How to apply it

  1. Name at least one cost of using the power that is active right now; it does not have to be the cost the power started with, but the power must never be free at its current tier.
  2. Make sure the cheap version of the power (the one with no limit) is always technically available, so choosing the limited version is a real decision, not a forced one.
  3. Give the current limit a visible, on-screen consequence at least once, rather than leaving it as a stated rule nobody has paid.
  4. Pick which cost type the power draws on, and let it show on screen: the body (the use itself does physical damage, as with Rock Lee's Eight Gates), the ability's own limits (a crude or incomplete version of the power rather than its full form, as with Yuji's Divergent Fist), or the mind (a cost paid in restraint and judgement, as with Ichigo's inner Hollow); a power may draw on more than one.
  5. When a character grows stronger and an old cost is retired, hand it a new cost at the new tier rather than letting the power reach a free ceiling: run the rotation the way One Piece's Gears retire one cost for the next, or the way Naruto's later forms each carry their own separate price.
  6. Sort every limit on the power into one of three kinds and write the label beside it: a limitation (what the power simply cannot do), a weakness (what an enemy can exploit) or a cost (what using it takes from the user). Sanderson's argument is that the three do different jobs, so a power carrying only one of them is thinner than it looks; he also holds that the plainest weakness, stripping the hero's powers in set circumstances, is a cliche worth replacing with something subtler.

The test

  1. Is there at least one cost of this power that is active right now, whether or not it is the cost the power started with?
  2. Is the cheap, unlimited version of the power always available, so restraint is a choice rather than a rule?
  3. Has the audience seen this limit actually cost the character something on screen, not just heard it described?
  4. Can you name which cost type is paying for this power: the body, the ability's own limits, or the mind?
  5. After the character's next power-up or form change, does a new cost take over, rather than the old one simply disappearing?
  6. For every limit on this power, can you say which of the three kinds it is, a limitation, a weakness or a cost, and does the power carry more than one kind rather than only the easiest one to write?

Failure mode

The character accumulates power with nothing currently at stake, so every fight's tension depends entirely on the plot choosing to make the character struggle; a viewer stops fearing for the character and starts merely watching, because the power itself no longer has a price. The clearest version of this symptom is a run of fights the character wins without taking any damage at all: every ability just works, nothing about using it costs anything any more, and each new fight reads as a formality rather than a real question. There is an opposite symptom too, and Sanderson's argument for it is that a cost so drastic no character can ever pay it removes the power from the plot altogether: on the page it reads as a power everybody talks about and nobody uses, which costs the story as much as a power with no price at all.

Evidence

SourceTimestampsWhat it arguedVerdict

S-00110:16-13:44A protagonist's escalating power tiers each carry their own physical cost; the source concedes some early costs ease with growth, and argues there is always something left holding the character backsupports
S-00110:16-13:44A protagonist whose abilities have a fallback for every limitation walks away from a major fight with no meaningful cost, which the source argues makes the fight boringsupports (counter-example)
S-00200:36-01:51Rock Lee's Eight Gates buy him speed and power at a cost paid in his own body: opening them tears his muscles and breaks his bones as he keeps fightingsupports
S-00201:51-02:53Yuji's Divergent Fist is a workaround forced by an ability he cannot yet use in its intended form, so the cost sits in the power's own limits rather than in his body or his mindsupports
S-00202:53-03:49Ichigo holds back from using his inner spirit's power because losing control risks hurting the people he is protecting, a cost paid in restraint and judgement rather than the bodysupports
S-00205:32-08:34A protagonist whose every ability works exactly as intended, fight after fight, with no cost paid anywhere, reads as boring because the outcome is never in doubtsupports
S-00212:23-14:20Each new form carries its own distinct cost, and while some early costs ease as the character grows, the source argues there is always a limitation left in forcesupports
S-004Second Law, segments 9-17Limitations (what the magic cannot do), weaknesses (what an enemy can exploit) and costs (what using it takes) matter more than powers, and the three are different things: in Eddings's Will and the Word a practitioner cannot unmake a thing, a fight with Superman only turns tense once an enemy holds kryptonite, and the One Ring charges its bearer in growing covetousness and in being sensed by the enemy while worn. He calls The Wheel of Time's elemental palette generic and argues it becomes fascinating only once the men who use the male half of the magic go slowly insane, and he warns that a cost nobody can pay removes the power from the plotsupports

Disagreements

None yet.

A villain group is one force made of people you could each pick out of a line-up, and a member you have no screen time to make a person weakens the group; a faceless collective is a deliberate choice, never a default.

Contents
  1. Rule
  2. Why it works
  3. How to apply it
  4. The test
  5. Failure mode
  6. Evidence
  7. Disagreements
  8. In Hood Ninjaz

Rule

A villain organisation has to read as one force and as a room full of separate people at the same time. The force comes from a purpose the audience could state in a sentence after one scene. The people come from each member carrying something that is theirs alone, a want, a method, an idea they embody, so that nobody in the group is merely the other one. That second half is bought with screen time and nothing else, which means the roster is priced by the time available: every member added past that point arrives as a name rather than a person, and spends credibility the developed members earned. The exception is deliberate and rare. Where the group's job in the story is scale, a tide rather than a set of antagonists, individuality is the wrong tool, and giving each member a face would shrink the very thing that makes them frightening. Decide which of the two you are writing before you name a single member, because the two designs pull in opposite directions and a group caught between them reads as neither.

Why it works

An audience cannot hold a roster, it holds people, so the organisation survives in memory only through whichever members the story managed to turn into people. A shared purpose does the unifying work cheaply, in a line, but distinctness has to be paid for in scenes, and there are only so many scenes. Roster size is therefore a budget question: divide the time available by the number of members and the answer is how much person each one can be. Past the point where that division stops producing people, extra members do not add threat, they dilute it, because the audience begins filing each new arrival as more of the same and stops expecting anything from the next one. The faceless collective works for the opposite reason: when the intended feeling is scale, sameness is the effect, and the moment one member becomes a person the reader starts measuring the threat by that person instead of by the size of the thing behind them.

How to apply it

  1. Decide which kind of group this is before writing a member: a cast of antagonists the reader will name, or a faceless collective whose whole job is scale. The two are built differently and the choice does not survive being made halfway through.
  2. Write the group's purpose in one sentence a reader could repeat back after a single scene, and check every member's behaviour against it, so the unit is established before any individual is.
  3. Count the scenes the group actually has, then set the roster to that, not to the size the organisation would realistically be.
  4. Give each member one axis that is theirs alone and cannot be traded: Fullmetal Alchemist hands each of its Homunculi a name from the deadly sins and then makes the method match the sin, and Bleach gives each Espada a different aspect of death to embody.
  5. Put the whole roster in one room on the page and cut any member who could not be picked out of that room without their power being named.
  6. If the group is the faceless kind, keep the individuals out on purpose: uniform behaviour, uniform speech, no member handed a private want, and any exception written as a deliberate break rather than the start of a cast.

The test

  1. Can you say what this group stands for in one sentence without naming a member?
  2. Is the roster bigger than the time you have to develop it?
  3. Take any member out of the group and describe them alone: is there anything there that no other member has?
  4. Could two members swap their dialogue in a scene without a reader noticing?
  5. If the group is meant to be faceless, has any member acquired a want, a voice or a face the reader could hold on to, and was that break deliberate?

Failure mode

A reader finishes the arc able to name the leader and maybe a couple of the others, and cannot say who the rest were or what any of them wanted. The group reads as strong on the page and hollow in memory. The clearest tell is a reader describing a member by their power alone, because the power was the only thing the story ever established about them. The second tell is that arrival scenes stop landing: each new member is met with recognition of a type rather than curiosity about a person, so the group's later reveals have nothing to land on.

Evidence

SourceTimestampsWhat it arguedVerdict
S-00301:14-03:37Rule one is individuality: a legendary villain organisation stands for something and feels like a unified force while every member feels like their own person. Worked through Hunter x Hunter's Phantom Troupe as a room of unmistakable individuals, Fullmetal Alchemist's Homunculi as figures built to carry one goal and each defined by a named deadly sin, and Bleach's Espada, the top-ranked Arrancar in Aizen's forces, each built around a different aspect of deathsupports
S-00303:38-05:37The counter-example from the same series: Bleach's Sternritter, a larger roster than the Espada, each granted a letter of the alphabet and an ability tied to it, are argued to arrive, show a wild power and vanish, so that by the end of the arc the presenter says he could not tell you who most of them are. He puts the thinning down to a shortened runway forced on the authorsupports (counter-example)
S-00305:38-07:13The deliberate exception: not every villain organisation needs a developed roster, and which it needs depends on the role that organisation plays in the story. Invincible's Viltrumites and Blame!'s Silicon Life are offered as groups whose weight is their scale, where the presenter argues that giving every member a distinct identity would destroy the feeling the story wants; he names sci-fi as the home of this designsupports
S-004Third Law, segment 22The same roster argument from a second family, reached from the worldbuilding side by a produced author writing about his own design. He argues that strength comes from taking one or two things the story already has and extrapolating them hard rather than adding more, and he offers the more-is-more reflex in the third Spider-Man film as the warning, holding that one dangerous and compelling villain often makes a better story than a crowd of them. Independently, too many villains was indeed that film's most common criticism, though its reception was mixed rather than a panning. His rule is a practitioner's craft argument, not a finding about audiencessupports

Disagreements

None yet.

Every member of a villain group changes the heroes' story in a way no other member does; if two members leave the same mark, one of them is a wall, not a villain.

Contents
  1. Rule
  2. Why it works
  3. How to apply it
  4. The test
  5. Failure mode
  6. Evidence
  7. Disagreements
  8. In Hood Ninjaz

Rule

A villain group earns its place by what it does to the heroes, one member at a time, and each member must change the heroes' story in a way that is theirs alone: a wound, a betrayal, a question a hero cannot answer, a truth that rewrites what a hero thought had happened. The test is subtraction. Cut a member out and something in the heroes' story has to go missing with them; if the story closes over the gap unchanged, that member was scenery with a name and a power. Two members who leave the same mark are one villain and one wall, and the fix is to cut one or give one a different job, never to make the second one louder or stronger. Where P-005 caps how many members a group can carry, this rule decides what each of those members is for.

Why it works

An audience does not track a roster, it tracks changes to the people it cares about. A member whose only function is to be harder than the last one is measured on a single axis, so the audience knows what he is for before he opens his mouth and the only live question is how long he takes to fall. A member who leaves his own mark makes the heroes' future different, so the shape of the story cannot be predicted from the fight. Distinct marks also make the group larger than the sum of its members: the heroes come out of the arc carrying several different injuries, and the group becomes the one thing that did all of them. And the rule defends the roster from padding, because a writer who cannot name a member's mark has just been told that member is not needed yet.

How to apply it

  1. Write one line per member: the single change this member makes to a hero that no other member makes. If the line will not come, the member is not ready to be written.
  2. Name whose story each mark lands on. A mark on "the heroes" in general is not a mark.
  3. Cut or merge any member whose line duplicates another's, merging into one stronger character rather than keeping both.
  4. Vary the kind of mark, not only its size: a personal loss, a belief put under attack, a revelation that reframes the past, a betrayal that changes the shape of the plot.
  5. Run the subtraction test on every member before drafting their arc: delete them and read the heroes' story back. Whatever goes missing is their mark.
  6. Give the walls a job instead of a promotion. An obstacle that exists to be beaten is fine as staging, as long as it is not sold to the audience as a member of the group.

The test

  1. Can you state in one sentence the change this member makes to a named hero?
  2. Is that change different in kind from every other member's, rather than the same change at a higher intensity?
  3. If this member were deleted, would something in the heroes' story be missing?
  4. Do the marks land on different heroes, or on different parts of one hero, rather than all on the same nerve?
  5. Read the members' arcs in order: does each one end somewhere the previous one did not?

Failure mode

Every appearance runs the same beat in the same order: the sympathetic past, the fight that pushes the heroes past their limit, the defeat. Members can each be a good villain and the group can still fail this test, because the failure is structural rather than individual: no single member is badly written, and the repetition is in the pattern they are all cut to. A reader notices it as flattening. By the third or fourth arrival they can predict the shape of the arc from the member's first appearance and be right every time, so they stop asking what this one will cost the heroes and start asking only how strong he is.

Evidence

SourceTimestampsWhat it arguedVerdict
S-00308:39-11:28The model: a squad of rogue ninja hunting the world's most powerful creatures for a plan to reshape it, whose members each change the story differently. Itachi is presented as the killer of his own clan, which drives Sasuke's revenge across hundreds of chapters until the reveal that he acted to stop a coup turns Sasuke against his own village instead. Pain destroys that village and kills people close to Naruto, then puts the cycle of hatred to him as an argument. Zetsu is secretly serving the final boss and betrays the group. The presenter's own claim, that no member is doing the same thing as another, is carried as his argumentsupports
S-00311:29-13:40The counter-example: the ranked demons serving Muzan, whom the presenter rates individually as good villains with memorable personalities and backstories, and whose contribution he argues is the same every time, a tragic past, the heroes pushed past their limits, defeat. His reading is carried as his. It is also weaker than he states it: one of the demons he lists as another tragic past was a criminal in his human life, so the pattern he names breaks on his own examplesupports (counter-example)

Disagreements

None yet.

The eye reads a group as a unit before the plot does, through a shared uniform, symbol or palette that each member's own silhouette still stands out inside; drop the shared mark and the group stops existing on screen.

Contents
  1. Rule
  2. Why it works
  3. How to apply it
  4. The test
  5. Failure mode
  6. Evidence
  7. Disagreements
  8. In Hood Ninjaz

Rule

A villain group has to be legible to the eye before it is legible to the plot, and that takes two things at once. One shared mark, a uniform, a symbol or a colour palette, carried by every member who appears on screen, so a reader meeting them for the first time files them as one force without being told. And one silhouette per member that the shared mark cannot swallow, so the group reads as a set of people rather than a rank of copies. Where the story genuinely forbids a uniform, the shared mark shrinks to something small and private and the silhouettes carry the rest of the load; it is not deleted. A group whose shared mark goes away, with nothing designed to replace it, stops existing on screen no matter what the script keeps calling it.

Why it works

A reader sorts a frame into sides before reading a word of it, so the design is the first statement the story makes about who these people are to each other. The shared mark does the group half of that job, converting a list of characters into one body with one intent. The distinct silhouette does the individual half, keeping each member recoverable inside the uniform so a reader can hold them apart in memory between appearances. The two halves are in tension by design: too much unity and the members blur into wallpaper, too much individuality and the organisation dissolves into a coincidence of people. This is not P-001 at group scale, and the two should not be run together: P-001 is the image of one power tied to one character, and this page is the image of one group, so every member can pass P-001 while the group still fails here. What makes the shared mark expensive to abandon is that it does its work cumulatively: the audience spends a whole series learning to read it, and once learned, the mark alone is enough to raise the threat before a single member is named.

How to apply it

  1. Choose one shared mark for the group and own it exclusively: a garment, a symbol or a palette that no other faction in the story uses.
  2. Put the mark in every scene the group appears in, including the scenes where only one member turns up, so it stays the group's signature rather than a meeting-room costume.
  3. Give each member one feature at silhouette level, not colour level, that the shared mark cannot hide: build, headgear, a carried weapon, a body that is not human standard. Naruto's Akatsuki are the model, with the black robe with red clouds sitting over a shark-like body, a scorpion-like puppet shell, a scythe carried on an extendable rope, and a nonhuman member built on plant biology.
  4. Draw the roster as filled black shapes at thumbnail size and check no two match. If two match, change a silhouette, never a colour.
  5. If the group must work unseen, shrink the mark instead of deleting it, and raise the silhouette work to carry what the uniform no longer carries. The source offered the Phantom Troupe as its example of a covert group and the fact check refuted that: the Troupe are feared worldwide, so they are not covert, but they do show the shrunken-mark form, one shared tattoo in place of a uniform.
  6. If the shared mark is ever retired inside the story, design its replacement in the same beat, and check the replacement is a mark and not just a plot reason for its absence.
  7. Keep every member's design in one visual language. New members join the language rather than importing their own.

The test

  1. In a frame with no dialogue and no name captions, would a first-time reader place these characters as one organisation?
  2. Is there a single shared mark, and does every member who appears on screen carry it?
  3. At thumbnail size, in filled black shapes only, can you tell every member apart?
  4. Does each member keep one feature the shared mark cannot hide?
  5. If the group works unseen and wears no uniform, is there still one small shared mark, and are the silhouettes doing more work because of it?
  6. If the shared mark is dropped at any point in the story, does something else take over its job in the same beat?
  7. Does every design in the group belong to the same visual language as the others?

Failure mode

It arrives in two steps and the second one is what a reader actually notices. First the unifier goes, whether by plot reason or by drift, so nothing in a frame says these people are together. Then the individual designs, no longer being held in line by anything shared, start pulling against each other, and the reader's eye finds no place to rest and no way to file who is who. The symptom reads as a set of characters the script keeps calling an organisation while they never once look like one, and a reader who could name every member of the earlier group cannot reliably name two of this one. S-003 reads Boruto's Kara this way: its Inner members are documented as wearing dark cloaks with Roman-numeral facial tattoos and their own cloak linings, and the presenter's account is that the cloaks stop appearing and the remaining designs, mixing sci-fi body modification with clashing period and costume references, no longer read as one organisation. The dropping of the cloaks is his reading of the later art, not a recorded change.

Evidence

Naruto's Akatsuki are offered as the model, the black robe with red clouds unifying members whose own silhouettes stay distinctsupports (the claim that every member wears the robe is corrected on the source page)
S-00316:46-19:11Boruto's Kara is the counter-example: the presenter argues the group's cloaks stop appearing and the designs left behind clash, so the members no longer read as one organisation the way the Akatsuki still dosupports (counter-example)

Disagreements

None yet.

A power may solve a conflict only to the degree the audience already understands it; a power the audience does not understand may create problems and never solve them.

Contents
  1. Rule
  2. Why it works
  3. How to apply it
  4. The test
  5. Failure mode
  6. Evidence
  7. Disagreements
  8. In Hood Ninjaz

Rule

Understanding is the currency a power spends when it resolves a conflict, and the balance is whatever the audience has been shown before the scene begins. That gives a scale rather than a switch. At the understood end the audience knows the mechanism and its limits, so a solution reads as a character being clever with a tool the reader can check, and the reader gets to run slightly ahead of the page. At the unexplained end the power stays mysterious, and its job is to make things worse: it generates the problem, closes the exits, takes something away, and leaves the characters to get out on what they have. Both ends work, and a story can sit anywhere between them, so long as each system is spent at the rate it has been explained. What never works is a power paying out before the audience holds it, or a rule written into the system in the scene that needs it. Where a system is due to be revealed late, the reveal may cost the characters and must not rescue them. This rule and P-002 are two halves of one discipline: P-002 governs how a power is built, one mechanism used cleverly rather than a shelf to choose from, and P-008 governs when that mechanism may be spent on the plot, only once the audience already understands it.

Why it works

Tension is arithmetic the audience does itself. A reader who knows what a power can and cannot do is working the problem alongside the character, so a solution lands because it was available and they nearly saw it coming; a reader who knows nothing cannot be surprised, only informed. That is the mechanism under the old charge of the contrived ending: the audience is told after the fact that the thing which just saved everyone was possible all along, and that retrospectively empties every earlier danger of its weight. Mystery itself is not the fault, and holding rules back is not cheating, because an unexplained power keeps its full force as long as it is the thing that costs and never the thing that pays. The bill for an unearned rescue is not settled in the scene where it happens; it is settled in every scene afterwards, once the reader has learned that this story can produce whatever it needs.

How to apply it

  1. Decide before drafting which end of the scale each system sits on, and write the decision down: understood well enough to resolve a conflict, or mysterious and allowed to generate problems only.
  2. For every system on the understood end, list what the audience has actually been shown on the page rather than what exists in the notes. That list is the entire budget available for solving anything.
  3. When a character is stuck and the system is understood, ask what they could do with what they already have and know, then make them do that instead of handing them something new.
  4. When a character is stuck and the system is mysterious, ask how attempting the power here could make things worse, and take that route rather than the rescue.
  5. Never write a new rule, tier or exception into a system in the scene that needs it. If the rule is real, plant it earlier, in a scene where it costs the characters instead of saving them.
  6. Where a late reveal is planned, schedule the explanation ahead of the payoff: the audience is given the rule in one scene and watches it pay in a later one, never both in the same beat.
  7. Test any power the audience does not yet understand against one question before it enters a scene: is it closing exits or opening them. Only closing is allowed.

The test

  1. For every beat where a power resolves something, can a reader point back at the earlier scene that showed them the rule which made it work?
  2. Does any character gain an ability, a tier or an exception at the moment of need, with no earlier plant?
  3. If the system is on the mysterious end, does it ever pay for the characters, or does it only ever cost them?
  4. Describe the resolution to someone who has read only to the halfway point: could they name it as a possibility?
  5. Is there a rule in the system that is used exactly once, in the scene it was written for?
  6. Where an explanation and a win land in the same scene, was that deliberate, and does the win still work if the explanation moves earlier?

Failure mode

The rescue nobody could have predicted, and the flattening that follows it. A reader reaches the resolution and says they did not know it could do that, and from that moment the earlier danger stops being dangerous on a reread. The visible tells are a power that appears at the moment of need and is never used again, an explanation delivered in the same breath as the victory, and a character asking what is happening while the system acts for them. The quieter tell is worse: readers stop guessing. Once a story has produced one unearned answer, the audience stops running ahead of it, and every set-up after that lands on nobody.

Evidence

SourceTimestampsWhat it arguedVerdict
S-004First Law, the law and the panelHe states the law that an author's ability to solve conflict with magic is proportional to how well the reader understands it, and answers the objection that stated rules cost a story its wonder.supports
S-004First Law, Soft MagicSoft magic holds its rules back to buy wonder, so its operating rule is that the magic creates the protagonists' problems and never solves them, with Tolkien read at that end.supports
S-004First Law, Hard MagicHard magic states its rules up front so a solution can read as cleverness, hard meaning understood by the reader rather than scientific, with Asimov's robot stories offered as the model.supports, with the Asimov claim narrowed
S-004First Law, The Middle GroundMost writing sits between the ends, and he reads Rowling as hard in the specifics and soft in the big picture while placing his own explicitly ruled Mistborn system near the hard end.supports, as the author's reading
S-004First Law, How To Use ThisThe desk instruction: choose the feel first, do not solve a problem with an aspect of a power the audience has not been shown, do not hand the heroes a new ability whenever they need one, and never write a law into the system for one situation.supports

Disagreements

None yet.

Before adding a new power, faction or rule, deepen the ones the story already has: extrapolate what they do to the world, interconnect them, and consolidate what does the same job.

Contents
  1. Rule
  2. Why it works
  3. How to apply it
  4. The test
  5. Failure mode
  6. Evidence
  7. Disagreements
  8. In Hood Ninjaz

Rule

When a story needs something new, a fresh threat, a texture, a reason a scene can happen at all, the first move is not invention but extraction: take what the world already contains and ask what it has not yet been made to do. Three operations do that work, in order. Extrapolate: follow one element the audience already knows out through the society, the culture, the ecology and the economy, until it has changed how ordinary people work, trade, marry and believe, and keep chaining the question rather than stopping at the first consequence. Interconnect: make the elements you keep answer to one idea, so the world reads as a single thing with several faces instead of a shelf of separately interesting ideas. Consolidate: set the elements side by side, and where two of them do the same job in the story, cut one and hand its material to the other. Only when all three are exhausted has a story earned the right to add, and the thing added is then extrapolated on arrival like everything else. The rule is not a ban on scale. It is an order of operations: go as big as the story needs, as long as the depth is bought first.

Why it works

A reader's sense of a world's size comes from consequence, not inventory, so one element that has visibly bent the society reads larger than several that touch nothing. Every new element also has to be understood before it can carry a scene, which means breadth spends the reader's attention on introductions and leaves none for what those introductions were for. Extrapolation is cheap by comparison because the reader is already carrying the element, so each new answer arrives as a discovery about something known rather than as one more thing to learn. Interconnection does the same work at the scale of the whole: elements answering to one idea compound in the reader's head, while unrelated ones have to be held separately and are dropped separately. Consolidation converts a redundancy into depth, because material spread thinly across two elements lands on one instead. This is the system-wide form of two rules the library already holds, P-002 on one mechanism used cleverly beating a toolbox chosen from, and P-005 on a roster being priced by the time available to make its members people; P-009 says the same of a world, where the budget being spent is the reader's attention.

How to apply it

  1. Before adding anything, list what the world already has and what each element has not yet been made to do, then add only what that list genuinely cannot supply.
  2. Extrapolate one element at a time through society, culture, ecology and economics, and chain the question outward: an ability that feeds an army changes how wars are fought and who can afford to fight one, not just how a single scene is won.
  3. Push every extrapolation down to ordinary life, to a job somebody does, a thing a religion says, a price somebody pays, because that is where a reader feels a world rather than hears about it.
  4. Interconnect what you keep by giving the separate systems one shared idea and naming them off it, the way Mistborn's single-metal abilities are named after roles in a thieving crew, so a reader meeting the newest one already knows what kind of world it belongs to.
  5. Streamline: where two elements do the same job in the story, cut one and give its material to the other, and treat an element that is inert now on the promise that it will matter later as the first candidate for the cut.
  6. When you do add, add for a job nothing existing could do, and extrapolate the new element the moment it arrives so it never sits in the world as an unexploited entry.

The test

  1. Name the newest thing you added to this world: could an existing element, extrapolated, have done that job?
  2. For each system in the world, can you say in one sentence what it has changed about how ordinary people work, worship, eat or trade?
  3. Do the elements share an idea a reader could state after meeting two of them, or is each one interesting only on its own terms?
  4. Are two elements doing the same job in the story?
  5. Is anything in the world present only for what it will do later, and doing nothing on the page now?
  6. Has the consolidating gone the other way, so that one character now carries every capability, or the cultures differ only in surface paint?

Failure mode

The reader can list what the world contains and cannot say what any of it has done to the people living in it. The tell is that each system arrives with an explanation and no consequence, so the story stops for a tour and resumes unchanged; the second tell is that the newest element is met with recognition of a type rather than interest, because the reader has learned that new things here do not go anywhere. The author names the habit Worldbuilder's Disease, worldbuilding practised in isolation from the rest of the craft, and hedges that the balance only matters to a writer who means to be published.

Consolidating too hard fails in two opposite directions, and both show on the page. In the first, everything has been loaded onto one protagonist because that was the tidiest place to put it, and the rest of the cast has nothing left that is theirs. In the second, the world has been thinned until every culture is the same culture in different paint, so travelling across it teaches the reader nothing.

Evidence

SourceTimestampsWhat it arguedVerdict
S-004Third Law, "The Law"The law itself: expand what you already have before you add something new. Offered as the author's own design philosophy, found by identifying weaknesses in his own work, and hedged as a guideline rather than a rule binding on anyonesupports
S-004Third Law, "Worldbuilder's Disease"The named failure: worldbuilding practised in isolation from the rest of the craft, softened into a warning about a bodybuilder skipping leg day, and qualified as mattering only to a writer aiming at professional publicationsupports
S-004Third Law, "Depth over breadth"Strong storytelling comes from changing one or two known things thoughtfully and extrapolating, against a more-is-more reflex. His case is Spider-Man 3, whose most common criticism was that it carried too many villains, where he argues that one dangerous and compelling villain would have made the better story. He also points at early superhero comics for the same habit, a generalisation with no title named behind it, so it is carried as his argument onlysupports
S-004Third Law, "Extrapolate"The first operation: chain what-happens-when questions out through society, culture, ecology and economics instead of handing new powers to more characters, since a world is memorable for how deeply its elements are worked into everyday life. His worked examples are a wizard converting to Christianity, magic that creates food changing how armies move, and magic that drives its male users insane changing gender dynamicssupports
S-004Third Law, "Interconnect"The second operation, and his concession of the law's limit: a very large amount of worldbuilding still works where the elements interconnect thematically rather than reading as a pile of separately cool ideas. Discworld is his example of scale carried that way, and independently that series does grow its institutions rather than multiply them, the City Watch expanding from a handful of men into a full police force across the books. In his own Mistborn the single-metal abilities are named after roles in a thieving crew, Coinshot and Lurcher among them; the theming intent behind the naming is his own testimonysupports
S-004Third Law, "Streamline"The third operation: consolidate rather than proliferate, because one distinctive property can generate religions, social structures, conflicts and occupations across several societies. His worked case, told as his own account, is his editor Harriet McDougal telling Robert Jordan to cut Dannil, a young character doing nothing in the first The Wheel of Time book, answering the plea to keep the character for later books with the point that a first book nobody enjoys has no later books, after which that material was redistributed. He also names the two ways streamlining goes too far, everything loaded onto one protagonist and every culture identical but for surface paintsupports

Disagreements

Sanderson - Laws of Magic (three essays)

ID
S-004
Status
Details
Source
brandonsanderson.com, three essays. Sanderson's First Law, brandonsanderson.com, dated February, 2007 in the page's byline. Sanderson's Second Law, brandonsanderson.com, dated April 2011 in the page's byline. Sanderson's Third Law of Magic, brandonsanderson.com, September 2013, where the month and year are settled but the exact day is unconfirmed page furniture rather than a byline (see ## Corrections)
Speaker
Brandon Sanderson, a produced fantasy author writing about his own design principles. A practitioner's track record, not a critic's argument, which is why this library may weigh his craft rules as a second source family. He hedges all three laws himself, calling them "observations about what have made my own magic systems better" rather than rules anyone else must follow
Why it is filed
the first source family in this library outside the Pavelover channel, and the first practitioner. Three constraint laws in one place: understand the magic before it may resolve anything, limitations over powers, expand what exists before adding anything new
Ingest method
WebFetch of each essay on 2026-09-05, then a targeted second pass per essay to settle disputed lines. No verbatim text was saved, on copyright grounds: the scratchpad record holds the argument in order, the claim list and eight one-sentence attributed quotes, and this page carries at most those eight plus the author's hedge on the laws' status. No raw material entered the repo
Cleaning note
the promotional opening of the Third Law (the new novel, the audiobook chapters, the trailer and the promotional hunt) and all three pages' linked-article furniture stripped. The one two-sentence pull quote was trimmed to its second sentence to hold the one-sentence rule. Word counts are published nowhere on this page: the intake's figures count its own saved records, not the essays, and the essays' own lengths are unverified estimates
Verification
73 claims checked, 26 verified, 4 corrected, 43 unverifiable (36 craft rules and opinions, unverifiable by design, plus 7 statements about other people's books that no independent source settles). Every fact about a reference work was re-verified against a source independent of the essay that asserted it, which moved 12 verdicts and most tiers from PRIMARY to SECONDARY. See ## Verification

Show all 26 rows
#TimeWhat it arguesFeeds
1first-law, IntroductionMagic is what marks fantasy out as a genre, and the laws that follow are guidelines and his own design principles rather than rules binding on anyone-
2first-law, The Law and the Worldcon panelHe states the Law, reports the panel that disagreed on the grounds that rules cost you wonder, and answers with Campbell's genre distinction and the deus ex machina chargeP-008
3first-law, Soft MagicSoft magic leaves the rules unexplained and buys wonder with mystery, so its operating rule is that magic creates the protagonist's problems and never solves themP-008
4first-law, Hard MagicHard magic states the rules up front so the reader can enjoy the cleverness of a solution, and hard means understood rather than scientificP-008
5first-law, The Middle GroundRowling is hard in specifics and soft in the big picture; he places his own systems well toward the hard end and holds background rules back for later booksP-008
6first-law, How To Use ThisPick the feel you want first, never introduce an unexplained power to solve a problem, and use the diagnostic question that matches your end of the scaleP-008
7first-law, Author's noteHe notes this is the second draft, that it will likely be revised, and that it probably has a lot of typos in it-
8second-law, IntroductionThe laws are personal design principles rather than absolute rules, and this one is a principle of storytelling generally that magic happens to show clearly-
9second-law, The LawLimitations matter more than powers, and Superman proves it because kryptonite and the Kent code reach back into his origin and upbringing while flight and strength say nothing about himP-004, CS-superman
10second-law, What This Means for WritersOriginality comes from limitations, which is why the story follows the hobbits and Aragorn's reluctance, and why a generic elemental magic becomes fascinating once the men who use it go slowly insaneP-004, CS-the-wheel-of-time
11second-law, StruggleLimitations force the characters to work harder and the author to write more cleverly, as when a practitioner can only push metal directly away or pull it directly toward the selfP-002, P-004
12second-law, TensionA limitation raises the dramatic stakes, because Superman fighting an enemy is not very tense until the enemy has kryptoniteP-004, CS-superman
13second-law, DepthA limitation forces the world and the character to be developed further, since a character who can fly is thin but one who can only fly when she is happy has depth forced on herP-004
14second-law, LimitationsLimitations are what the magic simply cannot do, and the good ones are tied to the nature of the world rather than arbitrary, as with a magic that cannot unmake a thingP-004
15second-law, WeaknessesWeaknesses are exploitable vulnerabilities, and the version that simply removes the hero's powers in certain circumstances is a cliche to be replaced with something subtlerP-004, CS-superman
16second-law, CostsCosts can be abstract, like the Ring's corrosion of its bearer, or concrete, like a tariff paid per casting, but a cost so drastic that nobody can pay it removes the magic from the plotP-004
17second-law, OthersAsk how the magic is accessed, powered and how often it can be used, avoid the standard answers, and choose answers that tie the magic to the settingP-004
18second-law, Not Just a Principle of MagicsThe law generalises to character, worldbuilding and plot, because what characters have trouble accomplishing is more interesting than what they do easilyP-004
19third-law, OpeningPromotional opening for the new novel, then the sequence framing and the note that he found the laws by spotting weaknesses in his own work-
20third-law, The LawExpand what you already have before you add something newP-009
21third-law, Worldbuilder's DiseaseWorldbuilding practised in isolation from the rest of the craft is a disease, and the balance only matters if you want to be published professionallyP-009
22third-law, Depth over breadthStrong storytelling comes from changing one or two known things and extrapolating hard, against the more-is-more reflex that cost the third Spider-Man filmP-009, P-005
23third-law, ExtrapolateChain what-happens-when questions out through society, culture, ecology and economics rather than handing new powers to more charactersP-009
24third-law, InterconnectHe concedes his law's limit: a very large amount of worldbuilding works when the elements interconnect thematically, as his own abilities do when themed around the roles in a thieving crewP-009, P-002
25third-law, StreamlineConsolidate rather than proliferate, since one distinctive property can generate religions and occupations across societies, and cutting an inert character to redistribute his material strengthens the restP-009, CS-the-wheel-of-time
26third-law, ConclusionBalance depth against breadth, and his own worldbuilding got stronger when he stopped asking for more awesome magics and started asking what the common themes wereP-009

Corrections

No transcript here, so nothing is mis-heard. What needs correcting is a date the page does not carry and a title the essay transposes, with the basis for each.

WhereOn the pageCorrected
Third Law, the dateThe post body carries no date at all, only the signature. The only dates rendered on the page sit in the More articles block below it, Sep 24, 2013 on one card and Sep 26, 2013 on anotherSeptember 2013 stands, the exact day does not. The page's hidden structured data gives 2013-09-25, a 2014 archived capture of the old site layout displayed the post date as Sep 25, 2013, and the book the post promotes was published on 24 September 2013. The filename's 2013-09-24 is the earliest date rendered on the page, taken for sort order only, and is not a verified publication day (rows 51, 52)
First Law, Martin's seriesThe essay renders the title as A Song of Fire and IceA Song of Ice and Fire. Recorded as the source's own slip rather than corrected silently, because he flags the piece as a second draft likely to contain typos, so it may be his transposition rather than his source's. The wrong form is never reproduced on any other page in this library (row 11)

Two further items are excluded rather than corrected, because neither can be settled from what was fetched. A first fetch pass attributed a line about naming the powers after himself to the Third Law essay; the targeted second pass found no such line, so it is discarded and must not be used. And the joke notation printed alongside the Second Law's statement was confirmed on one pass only, so it is left out of the record entirely.
